exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Identity regimes: is KYC/CIP law for the sponsor or administrator, and what identity proofing is policy?
original_provisional_answer: Identity proofing is required for advisory-privilege holders and successors; sanctions screening for all parties. No CIP/AML programme unless counsel says one applies. Source-of-funds review only for complex assets and for contributions over a sponsor-set threshold.
recommended_answer: Confirm: CIP/AML program law does not apply to a 501(c)(3) sponsor or to a non-MSB software administrator (CIP is a bank/BD/fund rule; MSB AML applies only to MSBs). Policy controls: risk-based identity proofing for advisory-privilege holders, successors, and anyone granted payment-related authority; OFAC screening of donors, advisors, successors, grantees and payors of contributions at onboarding, on list updates, and before each grant; a written sanctions compliance program per OFAC Framework components for the sponsor, supported by platform logs. Change source-of-funds review from threshold-only to risk-based: complex assets, contributions above a sponsor threshold, AND pattern triggers below threshold (rapid in-out, third-party payors, structuring-like splits, high-risk geographies).
reconsideration_triggers: Operator or affiliate becomes MSB, RIA or BD
New FinCEN rule covering nonprofits or platforms
remaining_uncertainty: Full BSA 'financial institution' list (31 U.S.C. 5312(a)(2)) not fetched; bank/custodian contractual KYC expectations vary.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a new advisory-privilege holder or successor, When activated, Then identity proofing evidence is recorded.
Given any party (donor, advisor, successor, grantee, payor), When onboarded or before each grant, Then OFAC screening against the current SDN list is run and recorded with list version.
Given contributions below threshold, When pattern rules (third-party payor, rapid grant-out, split contributions) fire, Then a source-of-funds review case opens.
Given an OFAC list update, When published, Then all active parties are rescreened within the sponsor-set window.
supporting_interpretation: No statutory CIP applies to sponsor or software administrator; identity proofing is a control justified by fraud, account-takeover, §4958/§4967 related-party controls, and OFAC strict liability.

alternative_design: A) No referral pay (recommended for release 1): zero cost, loses a distribution lever. B) Flat annual marketing/co-branding fees to firms (not individuals), not tied to contributions, FMV-documented, firm registered as commercial fundraiser where required: moderate cost, moderate exposure. C) Sponsor employs internal gift officers (employees excluded from CA/NY definitions; §3(e)(2) allows employees in overall fundraising without per-donation pay): higher fixed cost, lowest exposure. D) Advisor-managed DAF program where advisor is paid by client, not sponsor: no §4958(f)(8) status, but common industry practice of sponsor-paid advisor fees should be reviewed.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound itself pays nothing (software only); it hosts sponsor-configured referral programs, so the platform must enforce constraints for sponsors.

authoritative_findings.claim: Any grant, loan, compensation or similar payment from a DAF to a donor, donor-advisor, family member or 35% controlled entity is an excess benefit transaction in full.
A donor-advisor includes any person appointed or designated by the donor with advisory privileges.

An investment advisor compensated by the sponsor for managing or advising on DAF assets (and family/35% entities) is a disqualified person of the sponsor, so sponsor payments to it are subject to §4958 excess-benefit (fair market value) review.
Proposed (not effective) regulations would treat such a sponsor-compensated personal investment advisor as a donor-advisor of the DAF it manages; no finalization or withdrawal found as of late 2026.

If the sponsor maintains a §3(c)(10)(B) pool, its broker-dealer exemption requires that persons soliciting donations to the fund receive no commission or special compensation based on the number or value of donations.
California: any person who for compensation solicits funds in California for charitable purposes is a commercial fundraiser and must register before soliciting (charity employees excluded).
California fundraising counsel excludes an investment counselor advising a client only when giving investment/financial advice; counsel must not solicit.
New York: any person who for compensation solicits on behalf of a charitable organization is a professional fund raiser; bona fide charity employees excluded.

Interpretation: a financial advisor paid by a sponsor for referring donors to open or fund DAFs is soliciting funds for charitable purposes for compensation, and so is a commercial fundraiser (CA) / professional fund raiser (NY) unless an exclusion applies; per-contribution or percentage fees are the clearest case.

business_assumptions: Referral payments, if any, are made by sponsors from operating funds.
Many referrers are wealth advisors who may also manage DAF assets for the sponsor.
competing_interpretation: A referral that merely introduces a client without the referrer asking for a contribution may not be 'solicitation' in some states; flat marketing-services fees unconnected to contributions may fall outside. FINRA/SEC rules may separately limit registered representatives' outside compensation (not surveyed).
consequences_if_wrong: §4958 excise taxes on the advisor (25%/200%) and managers (10%); loss of sponsor's §3(e) broker exemption for pooled funds; state penalties for unregistered solicitation; reputational harm.
conservative_fallback: No referral compensation at all; advisors participate only via their client-paid advisory fees (not paid by sponsor).

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Add both: per-donation compensation to solicitors jeopardizes the sponsor's broker-dealer exemption for pooled funds; sponsor-paid investment advisors of DAF assets are disqualified persons.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Does not mention Exchange Act §3(e)(2) or §4958(f)(1)(F)/(f)(8) investment advisor disqualified-person status.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: State the precise statutory class.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Accurate but scoped by §4958(f)(7) (donor, donor-designated advisor, family, 35% entity); 'advisors' should be read as donor-advisors, with financial advisors covered only if donor-designated (or under proposed regs).
corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: XID-CRM-002 rationale 'Payments from DAF assets to advisors or related persons are automatic excess benefit'

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Referral compensation to advisors/affiliates from sponsor operating funds: solicitor registration and §4958 exposure.
external_authorization_required: State registration of each compensated referrer where it solicits (California Registry of Charities and Fundraisers commercial fundraiser registration; New York professional fund raiser registration with the Charities Bureau); sponsor board/committee approval of disqualified-person compensation.
jurisdiction: US federal tax and securities; California and New York solicitation law; other states via jurisdiction table
landscape_update_candidates: Exchange Act §3(e)(2) bars commission/per-donation compensation to solicitors for sponsors maintaining §3(c)(10)(B) pools — relevant to industry advisor referral programs.
original_provisional_answer: No referral compensation is ever paid from fund assets. Flat, fair-market-value fees paid from sponsor operating funds under a written agreement are permitted only to persons who are not advisors or related parties of the referred fund, only in states whose paid-solicitor rules the table records as satisfied, and never per grant or per dollar granted.
recommended_answer: Confirm with tightening: (1) never pay any referral or compensation from DAF assets to anyone who is a donor, donor-advisor, their family, 35% entity, or a sponsor-compensated investment advisor of that fund (§4958(c)(2); proposed regs would extend). (2) Sponsor operating-fund payments to disqualified persons (incl. §4958(f)(8) investment advisors) must be FMV and documented (rebuttable-presumption process). (3) No compensation based on number or value of contributions to anyone soliciting where the sponsor maintains a §3(c)(10)(B) pool (EA §3(e)(2)); recommend this as a universal rule. (4) Any paid referrer who solicits in CA must be a registered commercial fundraiser (or the arrangement redesigned so the payee does not solicit), and in NY a registered professional fund raiser; other states via jurisdiction table defaulting to 'registration required'. Release 1: referral compensation disabled; flat, non-contingent, FMV fees enabled only after the referrer's state registration evidence is recorded.
reconsideration_triggers: Finalization or withdrawal of proposed §4966 regulations
Expansion into states without table entries
Change in referrer business models (e.g., RIA firms receiving sponsor-paid management fees)

related_question_answers.answer: CA (§12599) and NY (§171-a(4)) treat compensated solicitation for a charity as commercial/professional fundraising regardless of whether payment is per contribution; per-contribution pay is the clearest trigger and also breaches Exchange Act §3(e)(2) where the sponsor has a §3(c)(10)(B) pool. Other states: default registration-required in the table.

remaining_uncertainty: State-by-state treatment of pure referrals; FINRA outside-activity rules; whether proposed §4966 regs will be finalized; FMV benchmarks.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a payment from a DAF, When the payee is a donor, advisor, family member, 35% entity, or an investment advisor compensated for that fund, Then the payment is blocked.
Given a referral agreement, When the fee formula references contribution count, amount, or grant amount, Then activation is blocked.
Given a referrer soliciting in a state, When the jurisdiction table says registration required, Then fee payment is blocked until the referrer's registration evidence (number, expiry) is recorded.
Given a payee who is a disqualified person, When compensation is approved, Then FMV comparables and approval minutes are attached.
supporting_interpretation: Federal tax law prohibits any compensation from the DAF itself to donor-advisors; payments from sponsor operating funds are not automatic excess benefits but are subject to FMV review if the payee is a disqualified person (including §4958(f)(8) investment advisors). State solicitation law turns on compensated solicitation, not on source of payment.

alternative_design: A) Single-sponsor pools (release 1): low legal cost, duplicates investment operations per sponsor, loses scale economics. B) Host-sponsor multi-sponsor pool (one 501(c)(3) as trustee/administrator; participating-sponsor agreements; §7(e) disclosure by each): moderate cost (agreements, unitization, governance), large scale benefits for small sponsors, exposure low if conditions met. C) Registered fund/collective trust via bank or registered investment company: higher cost, no exclusion reliance. D) No pools; sponsor-selected mutual funds/ETFs per fund: lowest legal exposure, less customization.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound as multi-sponsor platform could technically offer a host-sponsor pool; operator must never be the pool's trustee/adviser for compensation tied to assets, and any paid solicitor of donations to a pooled fund would jeopardize the sponsor's §3(e) exemption.

authoritative_findings.claim: ICA §3(c)(10)(B) excludes a collective fund 'maintained by a charitable organization exclusively for the collective investment and reinvestment of' (among others) 'assets of the general endowment fund or other funds of one or more charitable organizations'.

A fund is 'maintained' by a charitable organization if the organization serves as trustee or administrator, or has the power to remove the trustees or administrators and designate new ones; 'charitable organization' means a §170(c)(1)-(5) or §501(c)(3) organization.
Each §3(c)(10)(B) fund must give each donor, at the time of donation, written information describing the material terms of the fund's operation.
Securities of a §3(c)(10)(B) fund are exempt securities under the Securities Act.

The charity (and its personnel) acting as trustee/administrator of a §3(c)(10)(B) fund is not a broker/dealer, but only if every person soliciting donations to the fund is a volunteer or in overall fundraising and receives no commission or special compensation based on the number or value of donations.
Charitable advisers advising such funds are exempt from registration; the exemption does not cover non-charity vendors.

Interpretation: a pool maintained by one 501(c)(3) sponsor holding DAF assets of several 501(c)(3) sponsors is within the text of §3(c)(10)(B)(i) ('one or more charitable organizations'); DAF assets are owned by the sponsor, so they are 'other funds' of a charitable organization.

Interpretation: an operator acting as 'administrator' does not by itself defeat the exclusion if a charity holds the power to remove and replace it, but the operator then performs adviser/broker-type functions without §203(b)(4)/§3(e) coverage.

business_assumptions: Each sponsor is a 501(c)(3) public charity.
Pool investment management is by the sponsor or an SEC-registered adviser/OCIO engaged by the sponsor.
Donor disclosure documents are sponsor-issued.
competing_interpretation: Participating sponsors' interests in a host-sponsor pool are themselves securities sold to other charities; Securities Act §3(a)(4) exempts them, but state securities regulators and anti-fraud rules still apply; the Philanthropy Protection Act's state-law provisions and any state opt-outs were not verified here. Whether an operator-administered pool is 'maintained' by a charity when the charity's removal power is merely contractual is untested.
consequences_if_wrong: Pool could be an unregistered investment company and its interests unregistered securities; sponsor could lose §3(e) broker exemption if solicitors are paid per donation.
conservative_fallback: Single-sponsor pools only, maintained by the sponsor as trustee, with §7(e) disclosure delivered at contribution and no transaction-based compensation to anyone soliciting contributions.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Multi-sponsor pools maintained by a charitable organization fall within §3(c)(10)(B)(i) ('one or more charitable organizations'). Prohibition in release 1 is a business-policy choice, not a legal requirement.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: States 'an operator-maintained or multi-sponsor pool falls outside' §3(c)(10)(B).

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Verified: Pub. L. 104-62 (Dec. 8, 1995) added ICA §3(c)(10)(B)-(D) and §7(e), Securities Act §3(a)(4) fund clause, Exchange Act §3(e), Advisers Act §203(b)(4).
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Unverified citation.
corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: XID-INV-003 authority 'Philanthropy Protection Act of 1995 (general knowledge)'

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Add §3(e)(2): no commission or special compensation based on number or value of donations to anyone soliciting for a §3(c)(10)(B) fund; links to XID-CRM-002.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Does not record the Exchange Act §3(e)(2) solicitor-compensation condition.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: What securities-law basis supports each pooled option, and may pools hold assets of more than one sponsor?
external_authorization_required: Sponsor board resolution establishing the pool and its investment policy; for multi-sponsor pools, executed participating-sponsor agreements; SEC-registered adviser engagement for any non-charity manager.
jurisdiction: US federal securities law; state securities law not surveyed
landscape_update_candidates: ICA §3(c)(10)(B)(i) expressly permits pools of 'one or more charitable organizations' maintained by a charity; relevant to shared investment pools across smaller DAF sponsors.
original_provisional_answer: Release 1: only single-sponsor investment pools maintained by the sponsor itself, relying on the charitable-organization exclusions added by the Philanthropy Protection Act of 1995 (Investment Company Act §3(c)(10)(B); Securities Act §3(a)(4)). Each pool records its legal basis; donors receive the written disclosure about the pool that the Act requires. Multi-sponsor pools and pools maintained by the operator are prohibited.
recommended_answer: Legal basis per pool: ICA §3(c)(10)(B) (exclusion), Securities Act §3(a)(4) (exempt security), Exchange Act §3(e) (sponsor not a broker/dealer, subject to §3(e)(2)), Advisers Act §203(b)(4) (sponsor personnel advice) plus registered adviser for any external manager, ICA §7(e) donor disclosure. Multi-sponsor pools ARE permitted by the statute when maintained by a 501(c)(3) sponsor (host sponsor as trustee/administrator or with removal power) and holding only charitable organizations' assets. Keep release 1 single-sponsor as a business-policy choice (operational simplicity), but record multi-sponsor host-sponsor pools as a legally available release-2 option rather than prohibited. Operator-maintained pools remain prohibited as policy (operator status risk).
reconsideration_triggers: SEC or state guidance on charitable pooled funds

related_question_answers.answer: Yes, under the statutory text: §3(c)(10)(B)(i) covers funds of 'one or more charitable organizations' maintained by a charitable organization, and 'maintained' includes serving as trustee/administrator or holding removal power. Conditions: only charitable-organization assets, §7(e) disclosure, §3(e)(2) compensation limit. Keep disabled in release 1 as business policy.

remaining_uncertainty: State securities law treatment of interests sold to participating sponsors; tax/UPMIFA governance of commingling across sponsors; whether a contractual removal power suffices for 'maintained'; no SEC staff letter on DAF multi-sponsor pools was retrieved.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a pool record, When activated, Then it names the maintaining charitable organization, the legal-basis list (ICA 3(c)(10)(B), SA 3(a)(4), EA 3(e), IAA 203(b)(4) or external RIA) and the role (trustee/administrator/removal power).
Given a contribution allocated to a pool, When accepted, Then the donor's §7(e) disclosure version is delivered and recorded at the time of donation.
Given a pool admitting another sponsor's assets, When enabled, Then a participating-sponsor agreement and both sponsors' 501(c)(3) status are recorded; release-1 configuration rejects this.
Given any person compensated for soliciting contributions to a sponsor with a pool, When compensation terms are recorded, Then they are not based on number or value of donations (EA §3(e)(2)).
supporting_interpretation: The statutory text expressly contemplates pools for 'one or more charitable organizations', and the maintenance test is satisfied by a charity acting as trustee/administrator or holding removal power. A host-sponsor pool admitting other sponsors' DAF assets is therefore available under federal law; the release-1 restriction is a business choice, not a legal requirement.

alternative_design: A) Descriptive-only (recommended): low cost, limited differentiation. B) Partner RIA supplies recommendations under its registration inside the UI with clear attribution and flat fees: medium cost, preserves AI-advice value. C) Affiliate RIA: high cost (registration, CCO, AML rule from 2028), maximum product freedom.
applicability_to_unbound: Covers AI assistant, analytics dashboards, rebalancing, model marketplace features.

authoritative_findings.claim: Adviser definition has three elements: compensation, being in the business, and advice/analyses/reports about securities.

Specific investment advice includes recommendations about specific securities or categories (e.g., mutual funds) and recommended percentage allocations; general allocation advice among securities, insurance and tangible assets is not specific.
Impersonal, regularly circulated publications are excluded; personalized advice attuned to a client's portfolio is not.
§203(b)(4) charity exemption does not cover a for-profit vendor.
If the operator or an affiliate registers as an RIA, the FinCEN investment adviser AML/CFT rule applies from its delayed effective date of January 1, 2028 (search-level verification only).

Interpretation: recommendation features (AI-suggested allocations, fund picks, rebalancing suggestions tailored to a DAF) for which the operator is compensated, even via a flat SaaS fee, satisfy the compensation element (any economic benefit) and likely make the operator an adviser; descriptive reporting of a fund's own holdings/performance without evaluation is lower risk but not categorically outside the 'reports concerning securities' prong.

business_assumptions: Sponsor or sponsor's RIA owns model selection.
Third-party data (e.g., fund factsheets) is displayed with attribution and without operator evaluation.
competing_interpretation: A flat SaaS fee still counts as compensation; analytics that score, rank, or flag holdings (e.g., risk scores, ESG ratings, drift alerts with suggested trades) could be 'analyses or reports concerning securities' issued as part of a regular business.
consequences_if_wrong: Unregistered adviser activity; required registration, compliance program, Form ADV, fiduciary duties, AML program from 2028.
conservative_fallback: Disable drift alerts with trade suggestions and any ranking/scoring of securities; show only sponsor-published materials.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Verified 15 U.S.C. 80b-3(b)(4) text; exemption limited to charitable organizations and their personnel.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Correct, now verified.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Does any platform recommendation feature make the operator an investment adviser?
external_authorization_required: None for descriptive-only features; SEC/state investment adviser registration of operator or affiliate if recommendation features are enabled (or executed agreement with a partner RIA that provides them).
jurisdiction: US federal (Advisers Act); state adviser laws not surveyed
landscape_update_candidates: FinCEN investment adviser AML rule delayed to January 1, 2028 (91 FR 36) — relevant to OCIO/RIA partners of DAF sponsors (search-level).
original_provisional_answer: The operator provides no individualized investment recommendations. AI and analytics features may only implement sponsor-approved models and display descriptive information. Operator compensation never varies with assets or trades. An affiliate RIA is out of scope unless the owner later chooses it.
recommended_answer: Yes, any feature that produces operator-authored, fund- or donor-specific recommendations on securities or allocations would likely make the operator an adviser (compensation via SaaS fee suffices). Confirm the decision: no individualized recommendations; AI may explain sponsor-approved options and execute sponsor-approved models; analytics limited to factual, non-evaluative reporting (holdings, performance vs sponsor-chosen benchmark, drift vs sponsor model) with no suggested trades except those mechanically required by the sponsor's model and approved by the sponsor. Third-party ratings may be shown only as attributed third-party content. Affiliate RIA remains a later business option.
reconsideration_triggers: Request for personalized AI investment suggestions
SEC guidance on AI/robo or analytics providers
remaining_uncertainty: Exact boundary for descriptive analytics under the reports prong; state law; how SEC would view AI explanation of options.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given an AI response about investments, When generated, Then it references only sponsor-approved options/models and contains no operator-originated recommendation to buy/sell/allocate (policy check logged).
Given an analytics view, When rendered, Then it contains factual metrics only and any rating is labelled with its third-party source.
Given a rebalancing action, When proposed, Then it derives mechanically from a sponsor-approved model and requires sponsor approval or sponsor standing policy.
supporting_interpretation: Removing individualized recommendations and limiting AI to executing sponsor-approved models plus factual reporting avoids the 'advice' element; flat fees avoid transaction-based compensation indicators.

alternative_design: A) Instruction-only relay (recommended): cost low, friction moderate (sponsor approval steps, sponsor-held credentials), exposure low, lost opportunity: no operator float income, no instant cross-sponsor settlement. B) Partner with licensed processor/transmitter for donor collection (e.g., processor as agent of payee of sponsor): cost per-transaction fees, friction low, exposure shifted to licensee, lost opportunity small. C) Obtain money-transmitter licences (~multistate NMLS, bonds, net worth, audits): high cost and 12-24 months, enables float and settlement products; not justified for release 1. D) Agent-of-payee structure where operator receives funds as sponsor's agent: legally available in MTMA states and CA (charitable services covered), but NY/FL lack a clean statutory equivalent and operator would carry custody/insolvency risk; reject for release 1.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound is software only; sponsors are 501(c)(3)s that own the money in sponsor-titled bank/custody accounts. Applies to all deployment models; highest exposure in embedded (host takes payments) and D2C (operator-branded collection) models.

authoritative_findings.claim: Federal money transmission requires acceptance of funds from one person and transmission to another location or person; status is facts-and-circumstances; there is also a catch-all for 'any other person engaged in the transfer of funds'.

Persons that only provide delivery, communication or network access services used by a money transmitter are excluded, and FinCEN says suppliers of software tools 'are engaged in trade and not money transmission'.

FinCEN analyses intermediaries by who owns the value, where it is stored, whether the owner interacts directly with the payment system, and whether the intermediary has 'total independent control over the value'.
FinCEN reads the exemptions strictly; a person cannot rely on one unless its activity conforms fully.

An ISO that 'does not take possession or control of merchant funds at any point' is not a money transmitter; for a processor serving mostly nonprofits collecting donations FinCEN found payment-processor conditions (a),(c),(d) apparently met.

Under the MTMA model, money transmission is selling/issuing payment instruments or stored value, or receiving money for transmission; it excludes the provision solely of online or telecommunications services or network access.
CSBS reports 31 states have enacted the MTMA in full or part (Nov 2026); Texas enacted full MTMA effective 9/1/2023; California enacted partial provisions; New York and Florida are not listed.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: CSBS Aug 2026 tracker; EV-D-005 page text

authoritative_findings.claim: California: 'services' for the agent-of-payee exemption include charitable activities of 501(c)(3) organizations (10 CCR §80.126.30, eff. 10/1/2021); DFPI found a company that received donations as the NPO's written agent exempt.

California: 501(c)(3) public benefit nonprofits that engage in money transmission are exempt (10 CCR 80.3002(a)(2)); a charity's payment processor must meet the statutory agent-of-payee test, common-law agency alone is insufficient.

New York: license required to receive money for transmission or transmit the same; agents allowed only as agent of licensee or payee. DFS staff: where funds go directly from payor's account to an account owned by the payee there is no receipt of money for transmission by the processor.

Florida: a money transmitter is an entity that receives value to act as an intermediary to transmit it, and 'includes only an intermediary that has the ability to unilaterally execute or indefinitely prevent a transaction'.
Texas MTMA agent-of-payee exemption at Fin. Code §152.004(2) requires a written agreement, holding out, and treatment of payment as received by payee.

Interpretation: an operator that never receives, holds, or has independent control over contribution or grant money, and whose software only transmits the sponsor's own authorized payment instructions to the sponsor's bank or custodian (sponsor-titled accounts, sponsor-held authority), is not 'receiving money for transmission' under the MTMA, CA, NY, TX or FL definitions, nor 'accepting' funds under 31 CFR 1010.100(ff)(5); it does not need the agent-of-payee or payment-processor exemptions.

Interpretation: the sponsor itself is not transmitting money for others when it grants its own funds (it owns DAF assets) and in CA is separately exempt as a 501(c)(3); consistent with prior internal REG-042.

business_assumptions: Contribution and grant accounts are titled to the sponsor (or custodian for the sponsor) in every deployment.
No operator-owned, FBO, omnibus or settlement account ever receives donor or grant money.

Payment execution requires sponsor-held authorization (sponsor approval or sponsor-configured standing policy executed under sponsor credentials); operator cannot unilaterally execute or indefinitely block a sponsor payment.
Card/ACH contributions settle directly from donor to sponsor-owned merchant/bank account through BSA-regulated institutions.
Operator fees are invoiced separately and never netted from charitable funds.
competing_interpretation: (1) The federal catch-all 'any other person engaged in the transfer of funds' and NY's 'or transmit the same' could be read to reach a party that originates transfers from another's account (e.g., via bank API credentials or ACH origination as a third-party sender) even without receipt. (2) If the operator holds credentials that let it initiate payments without contemporaneous sponsor approval, a regulator could find 'control' (FinCEN criterion d; Florida 'unilaterally execute'). (3) Embedded hosts or white-label partners that take donor money into their own accounts are themselves potential transmitters, and the operator could be seen as part of that flow. (4) Some non-MTMA states have broader definitions not surveyed here.
consequences_if_wrong: Unlicensed money transmission (state criminal and civil penalties; federal 18 U.S.C. 1960 exposure if MSB registration required and missing), forced restructuring of funds flow, bank partner termination.
conservative_fallback: Operate only models where all money moves between donor/sponsor/grantee accounts at BSA-regulated institutions under sponsor credentials; for any embedded host, contractually prohibit the host from receiving funds (or require host to be licensed/agent-of-payee of the sponsor under a written agreement satisfying MTMA §3.01(b)/CA §2010(l)).

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Say instead: donation processing has been treated as within the payment-processor/agent-of-payee frameworks in some rulings; but an instruction-only operator does not need either exemption because it never accepts funds.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Matrix states 'FinCEN's payment-processor exemption covers payments for goods or services, and a grant is neither.' FIN-2014-R009 (cited by XRA-008) treated donation processing for nonprofits as apparently meeting condition (a), and California regulation 10 CCR §80.126.30 defines 'services' to include 501(c)(3) charitable activities.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Cite FIN-2014-R009 for 'no possession or control = not a transmitter' (ISO activity) and FIN-2019-G001 §4.2 and §4.5.1(b) for control criteria and software-supplier treatment.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: R009 is an ISO/payment-processor ruling, not an instruction-only or software ruling.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Gate on FundsFlow conformance to the no-receipt/no-unilateral-control tests; require external licensing or licensed partner only when those tests fail.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Gate requires a 'multistate money-transmission memo' (paid counsel) before embedded/white-label deployments, regardless of whether the funds flow has any operator receipt.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Does instruction-only authority over sponsor-titled accounts keep the operator outside state money-transmission laws in target states?
external_authorization_required: None for a deployment that passes the no-receipt/no-unilateral-control tests. For any deployment where the operator or its affiliate receives or controls funds: state money-transmitter licences (via NMLS) and FinCEN MSB registration, or an executed agreement with a licensed transmitter/bank acting for the sponsor.
jurisdiction: US federal (BSA/FinCEN) and states; examples CA, NY, TX, FL; MTMA as model framework
landscape_update_candidates: CSBS (Nov 2026): 31 states have enacted MTMA in full or part; Texas full MTMA effective 9/1/2023; California partial (AB 1116 eff. 1/1/2025).

California 10 CCR §80.126.30 (eff. 10/1/2021) treats 501(c)(3) charitable activities as 'services' for agent-of-payee exemption; DFPI June 9, 2022 letter exempted a donation-routing rewards company acting as NPO agent.
Florida §560.103(27) limits money transmitters to intermediaries able to unilaterally execute or indefinitely prevent a transaction.
original_provisional_answer: Architecture rule: the operator never takes title to or possession of contribution or grant money; it holds instruction-only authority over sponsor-titled accounts. No embedded or white-label deployment that touches money goes live until a multistate money-transmission memo is on file.
recommended_answer: Confirm the architecture rule, with a sharper test: the operator stays outside federal MSB and state money-transmission definitions if (a) it never receives or holds donor/grant money (no operator, FBO, or pooled accounts), (b) it has no ability to unilaterally execute or indefinitely prevent a payment (sponsor-held bank/custodian credentials and approval; operator software only relays sponsor-authorized instructions), and (c) donor payments settle directly into sponsor-owned accounts through BSA-regulated processors/banks. Replace the gate 'multistate memo before embedded/white-label that touches money' with: a recorded FundsFlow conformance check against tests (a)-(c) plus a jurisdiction table (federal, MTMA states, CA, NY, TX, FL, others default-conservative). External legal authorization is required only for a deployment that fails (a)-(c): then use a licensed money transmitter or bank partner, or obtain licences.
reconsideration_triggers: Any proposal for operator-held, FBO, pooled, or settlement accounts, or netting of fees from charitable money
Operator obtaining payment-initiation credentials usable without sponsor approval, or acting as ACH third-party sender
Expansion to a state not in the jurisdiction table or whose MTMA version changes
New FinCEN ruling/guidance or state regulator action on software platforms or charitable payment facilitation
Embedded host or white-label partner that collects donor funds

related_question_answers.answer: Surveyed definitions (MTMA, CA, NY, TX, FL, federal) require receipt or control of money; instruction-only authority without receipt or unilateral execution ability is outside them. Map funds flow per deployment against those tests; only flows with operator receipt/control need licensing or a licensed partner.

remaining_uncertainty: No regulator ruling addresses a DAF software operator with instruction-only authority specifically. Non-MTMA, non-surveyed states may define transmission more broadly. Treatment of an operator acting as ACH third-party sender or holding API payment-initiation credentials is unsettled. Texas statute text was read only via bill analysis; California statute via mirror (official site blocked).
required_acceptance_criteria: Given any deployment, When its FundsFlow declaration is saved, Then every account holding contribution or grant money shows the sponsor (or custodian for the sponsor) as title holder and no operator/affiliate account appears; otherwise activation is blocked.

Given an operator service account, When it attempts to initiate a payment from a sponsor account without a sponsor approval record or sponsor-authorized standing policy, Then the request is rejected and logged.
Given operator billing, When fees are charged, Then they are invoiced to the sponsor and never netted from contributions or grants.

Given an embedded host, When the host integration is configured, Then donor payments settle directly to the sponsor's merchant/bank account and the host contract records that the host does not receive funds (or records host licence/agent-of-payee agreement).
Given a change to FundsFlow, When saved, Then the conformance check and jurisdiction table review re-run before activation.
supporting_interpretation: Every surveyed definition (federal and state) turns on receiving/accepting money and then transmitting it, or on control of the value. Florida expressly limits transmitters to intermediaries able to unilaterally execute or indefinitely block a transaction. FinCEN treats software/tool suppliers as engaged in trade. A pure instruction-relay with no receipt, no float, no pooled or FBO account, and no unilateral execution authority sits outside these definitions without needing any exemption. In California the sponsor (and its agents when it transmits) is additionally exempt as a 501(c)(3).

alternative_design: A) Software-only with sponsor/RIA decision ownership (recommended): low cost, moderate friction (sponsor approves models), low exposure, loses advisory revenue. B) Affiliate SEC-registered RIA providing models/advice to sponsors: high cost (registration, compliance program, FinCEN IA AML rule from 2028-01-01), enables AI recommendations and model revenue. C) Partner OCIO/RIA embedded under its own registration: medium cost via revenue share (must avoid transaction-based pay), low exposure. D) Broker-dealer partnership for execution: execution stays with registered BD; operator receives flat fees only.
applicability_to_unbound: Applies to investment-centric, advisor-distribution, white-label and HNW models (XRA-009/010). The operator has no §203(b)(4) or §3(e) coverage; the sponsor does.

authoritative_findings.claim: Investment adviser: any person who for compensation is in the business of advising others on securities, or who for compensation and as part of a regular business issues analyses or reports concerning securities; bona fide publishers excluded.
The charitable registration exemption covers only a charitable organization and its trustees, directors, officers, employees, volunteers; not a vendor.

SEC staff: 'in the business' if holding out as adviser, receiving separate or transaction-based compensation for advice, or giving specific investment advice (including recommended percentage allocations to particular fund types) other than on rare, isolated occasions.
Impersonal publications of general and regular circulation are excluded; advice 'attuned to any specific portfolio or to any client's particular needs' is adviser activity.

Broker = engaged in the business of effecting transactions in securities for the account of others; SEC staff indicators include compensation tied to transaction size/outcome, handling others' funds or securities, and operating platforms to trade securities.
The charity broker-dealer exemption covers the charity and its personnel only and is conditioned on no commission-based compensation to solicitors of donations to §3(c)(10)(B) funds.

Interpretation: features that create adviser risk for the operator are those that, for its fee, produce security- or fund-specific recommendations, allocations, model construction, manager selection, or evaluative ratings for a particular fund/sponsor; features that create broker risk are order routing/execution for others' accounts, holding securities or cash, or any fee varying with transactions, assets traded, or liquidation proceeds.

business_assumptions: Operator fees are flat or tiered SaaS fees not tied to AUM, trades, or liquidation proceeds.
Sponsors (or their RIAs/OCIOs) select and own investment menus and model portfolios.
Orders are executed by the sponsor's broker/custodian; operator never holds securities or cash.
competing_interpretation: The second prong of §202(a)(11) ('issues or promulgates analyses or reports concerning securities' as part of a regular business for compensation) can reach software that generates analytics about securities even without recommendations; staff and states have treated some technology/model providers as advisers. Generating and transmitting orders to a broker for a sponsor's account could be viewed as 'effecting transactions' by the operator if it, not the sponsor's custodian/broker, routes orders.
consequences_if_wrong: Unregistered adviser or broker-dealer activity (SEC/state enforcement, rescission risk, FINRA membership needed for broker), plus loss of sponsor exemptions if operator compensation taints §3(e)(2).
conservative_fallback: Ship release 1 with only sponsor-selected menus and descriptive reporting; no rebalancing automation that sends orders; order files exported to the sponsor's custodian for sponsor-initiated execution.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Correct and now verified: 15 U.S.C. 80b-3(b)(4) and 78c(e)(1) cover charitable organizations and their trustees/officers/employees/volunteers only.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: States 'Philanthropy Protection Act exemptions are for charities' without citation.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Add Type E (customizable SaaS/white-label for a charity) to the register; see XID-SAS-005 dossier.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Maps 'donation pages soliciting for multiple charities' to California platform registration; Type E (SaaS for a charity soliciting for itself) is not captured.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Which operator features create investment-adviser or broker-dealer status?
external_authorization_required: Only if disabled features are enabled: SEC (or state) investment adviser registration for the operator/affiliate, or broker-dealer registration and FINRA membership; otherwise none.
jurisdiction: US federal (Advisers Act, Exchange Act); state adviser/broker laws not surveyed
original_provisional_answer: Operator features are classified as follows: investment advice or model construction for compensation (adviser risk) — disabled; compensation varying with securities transactions or custody of securities (broker-dealer risk) — prohibited, operator fees are fixed SaaS fees; hosting donor solicitations (California platform risk) — see XID-SAS-005. A feature with an unmapped status question cannot be enabled.
recommended_answer: Confirm with refinements. Disabled unless an external registration path is chosen: (1) operator-authored recommendations, allocations, model construction, manager/fund selection, or ratings for a particular sponsor or donor; (2) operator order routing/execution where the operator is the party sending orders to market for others' accounts; (3) any operator compensation varying with AUM, trades, or liquidations; (4) operator custody of securities or cash. Permitted: implementing sponsor-selected models (sponsor approval recorded), producing order files or instructions that the sponsor's broker/custodian executes, factual/descriptive reporting of a fund's own holdings and performance without evaluative recommendation, generic educational content of general circulation. Each feature carries a status code in the OperatorStatusRegister; unmapped features stay disabled.
reconsideration_triggers: Product request for AI-generated recommendations or allocations to donors or sponsors
Pricing proposal with AUM or transaction components
Operator direct broker connectivity sending orders
SEC or state guidance on model-portfolio or analytics providers

related_question_answers.answer: A vendor that only executes sponsor-selected model portfolios, under sponsor approval, with flat fees and no recommendations, is not giving advice about securities to others for compensation (interpretation); keep execution with the sponsor's broker/custodian to avoid broker status.
See XID-INV-004 dossier: no individualized recommendations; descriptive analytics limited to factual reporting; flat fees.

remaining_uncertainty: No SEC statement specific to DAF platforms; boundary of the 'analyses or reports concerning securities' prong for descriptive analytics; state adviser definitions (Uniform Securities Act variants) not surveyed; staff positions on order-management software vendors not fetched.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a feature flagged adviser-risk or broker-risk in the OperatorStatusRegister, When a tenant enables it, Then activation fails unless a recorded registration path (affiliate RIA/BD or partner) is attached.
Given any model portfolio, When it is used for rebalancing, Then a sponsor approval record naming the model owner exists.
Given the operator's fee schedule, When computed, Then no fee component references AUM, trade count, trade value or liquidation proceeds.
Given an order generated by the platform, When released, Then it is executed by the sponsor's broker/custodian under sponsor authority, not submitted by an operator account.
supporting_interpretation: Status follows the operator's own conduct and compensation. Fixed SaaS fees that do not vary with trades or assets remove the strongest broker indicator and the 'transaction-based compensation' adviser indicator. Implementing a model selected and owned by the sponsor (or the sponsor's RIA) is acting on the client's investment decision, not advising.

B) Block CA for those models (prior decision): zero compliance cost, loses the largest US state market. C) Restrict to sponsor-owned platform pattern (sponsor domain, sponsor branding, listings only for advisory-privileged users): low cost, loses D2C brand. D) Seek written opinion: paid, excluded by zero-consultation budget.

authoritative_findings.claim: A charitable fundraising platform (CFP) is any person or entity that uses the internet to provide a website, service or platform to persons in California and performs, permits or enables listed acts, including (A) listing or referencing recipient charities by name to receive donations or recommended grants and (E) providing charities a customizable website/SaaS/platform to solicit or receive donations (not the charity's own platform, though it may integrate with it).

Excluded: a charity's own platform soliciting only for itself; a vendor that solely provides technical or supportive services (hosting, development, digital payment processing) to a CFP, unless it enables solicitation on its own platform; a DAF sponsor that solicits DAF accounts and receives grant recommendations and does not list recipient charities by name for persons without advisory privileges.

Solicitation types A-E in 11 CCR §314(m)-(q) track §12599.9(a)(1)(A)-(E); type E references private-labeled or customizable platforms and SaaS licence agreements; in type E a charity uses the CFP to solicit or receive donations for itself.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: ISOR pp.9-10; EV-D-029 FSOR Att. A resp. ~p.12

authoritative_findings.claim: CFP definition applies regardless of whether operated by charities or for-profits.

Obligations: register before soliciting/permitting/enabling solicitations, annual sworn reports, good-standing checks of charities (may rely on IRS/FTB/AG lists), conspicuous disclosures for types A-C, charity consent rules, prompt receipts for A/B; regs §§318-322 effective January 1, 2025.
Interpretation: the DAF-sponsor exclusion in (a)(2)(C) covers the sponsoring organization only; it does not exclude the operator.

Interpretation: a white-label or embedded deployment where the operator provides a customizable SaaS through which a sponsor solicits DAF contributions is within type E unless it qualifies as the sponsor's 'own platform'; the (a)(2)(B) vendor exclusion literally applies to vendors of a CFP, and an excluded DAF sponsor is not a CFP, so reliance on it is uncertain.
Interpretation: a D2C own-brand app that lists charities by name for grant recommendations, or a charity-side giving button network listing charities by name, is type A for the operator.

business_assumptions: California users will be served.
Charity directory/search shown only to authenticated advisory-privileged users in sponsor deployments.
competing_interpretation: A sponsor-licensed, sponsor-branded deployment on sponsor domains could be argued to be the sponsor's 'own platform' (excluded) with Unbound a technical vendor; and DAF account-holders recommending grants arguably are not 'donations solicited' by the platform when only advisory-privileged users see charity listings.
consequences_if_wrong: Unregistered CFP operation: AG enforcement, penalties, cease-and-desist (placement on May Not Operate list), sponsor reputational harm.
conservative_fallback: Register the operator as a CFP before any California deployment of any model and comply with type-A/E obligations; costs are filing fees and reporting.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Gate white-label and embedded the same way as D2C (registration or recorded sponsor-own-platform determination).
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Allows white-label and embedded to launch in CA without review, but the same record set (requirements/discovery/2026-11-23-cross-industry/13-BUSINESS-MODEL-ANALYSIS.md) flags CA Type E exposure for white-label and embedded, and §12599.9(a)(1)(E) expressly covers SaaS/customizable platforms for charities.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Which operating models make the platform company a California charitable fundraising platform (Type A/E) and what registration/disclosure follows?
external_authorization_required: Registration of the operator with the California Attorney General's Registry of Charities and Fundraisers as a charitable fundraising platform (initial registration form and annual renewal/report under §12599.9(b)-(c) and 11 CCR §315) before enabling type A or E solicitation for California users.
landscape_update_candidates: CA AG rulemaking (FSOR Att. A) confirms DAF sponsors acting as CFPs/platform charities may exercise variance power under 11 CCR §320(a)(3); type E expressly covers SaaS/white-label donation platforms.
original_provisional_answer: Assume the sponsor's California exclusion does not cover the platform company. D2C own-brand apps and charity-side giving buttons are not launched to California users until a California opinion is on file; other models may launch.
recommended_answer: Revise: (1) Sponsor-direct deployments where charity listings are visible only to advisory-privileged users and the experience is the sponsor's own branded platform: launch in CA with records showing sponsor ownership/branding (interpretation: excluded; moderate confidence). (2) White-label and embedded models: treat as potential type E. (3) D2C own-brand app and charity-side buttons: treat as type A. For (2) and (3), rather than block California indefinitely, register the operator with the Attorney General's Registry as a charitable fundraising platform before enabling, and implement §12599.9 duties (annual PL-4 report, good-standing checks via IRS/FTB/AG lists, type A-C disclosures, consent/removal handling, receipts where applicable). Registration is a filing, not a discretionary approval, so it removes the need for a paid opinion.
reconsideration_triggers: AG guidance or enforcement involving DAF software vendors
relevant_requirements: requirements/discovery/2026-11-23-cross-industry/13-BUSINESS-MODEL-ANALYSIS.md (D2C Type A; white-label and embedded Type E)
remaining_uncertainty: Whether white-label on sponsor domain is the sponsor's 'own platform'; fees and exact form numbers; how DOJ applies type E to DAF sponsors' contribution solicitation; vendor exclusion scope.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a deployment serving California users, When its model is D2C, charity-side button, white-label or embedded, Then activation requires a recorded CFP registration number and current renewal, or a recorded sponsor-own-platform determination.
Given a type A-C solicitation surface, When shown to a CA user, Then §12599.9(e) disclosures are displayed before donation/recommendation.
Given a recipient charity, When listed or granted to through a CFP surface, Then good-standing status (IRS, FTB, AG) is checked and recorded.
Given a charity's verified removal request, When received, Then its name is removed within three business days.
supporting_interpretation: Statute is broad and expressly targets SaaS/white-label (type E) and charity listings (type A); for-profits are covered; the DAF exclusion is entity-specific.

alternative_design: Live third-party verification API (e.g., Candid) at release: higher cost and vendor dependency, marginal freshness gain since IRS data are monthly.
applicability_to_unbound: Implement the freshness test as 'snapshot built from the most recent IRS posting (posting-date check) and retrieved within 24h'; store posting date, retrieval time and EIN/name match with each grant.

authoritative_findings.claim: TEOS/Pub 78 data, the EO BMF extract and the Auto-Revocation List are each 'generally updated monthly'.
IRS page states bulk data files are updated monthly; on 2026-11-24 Pub 78 and auto-revocation files were last updated 2026-11-11 and EO BMF 2026-11-10.

Sponsoring organizations may rely on listed public charity status for §4966 grantmaking; reliance continues until public announcement (or auto-revocation posting) unless the grantor knew, was aware of imminent revocation, or was partly responsible.
Reliance applies only to grants made in the organization's official/recognized name and not to group-exemption subordinates.
No IRS rule prescribes a 180-day deep-review interval or a 24-hour data freshness window; these are business controls.

business_assumptions: The platform ingests monthly IRS files promptly after posting.
Sponsors accept 180-day deep review as a default.
competing_interpretation: A 24-hour window adds operational dependency for little legal gain; checking that the snapshot equals the latest IRS posting (by posting date) is the legally meaningful test. Cross-sponsor evidence: reliance is defeated by knowledge, so a sponsor that receives an adverse public fact via the platform loses reliance for later grants - propagation is therefore protective.
consequences_if_wrong: Stale data could produce grants to revoked organizations; if sponsor knew, reliance fails and §4966 tax could apply.
conservative_fallback: Block release if the latest IRS posting date is newer than the snapshot's source date.

corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Correct that 180 days is not a legal standard, but the stated basis should be that reliance is tied to IRS publication/announcement dates (Rev. Proc. 2018-32 §§4-5), with data updated monthly.

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: What charity-status freshness and deep-review intervals apply, and can cross-sponsor evidence be relied on?
original_provisional_answer: Adopt RR-REQ-X-007-r1. An IRS-status check happens at approval and again at payment release, using an observation retrieved within the last 24 hours from the latest published TEOS/BMF/auto-revocation revision, with a per-sponsor snapshot. Deep review defaults to every 180 days (sponsor may tighten, not loosen), with automatic refresh starting 30 days before expiry. Cross-sponsor evidence may be reused as input only.
recommended_answer: Confirm with clarification: status check at approval and at release against the latest published TEOS/Pub 78, EO BMF and Auto-Revocation releases (record posting date; retrieval within 24h is an operational target, not a legal threshold); grant made to the listed legal/recognized name; group-exemption subordinates flagged for additional verification; deep review default 180 days (sponsor may tighten) with refresh 30 days before expiry; cross-sponsor evidence reused only as input, with any known adverse public fact always considered (knowledge defeats reliance).
reconsideration_triggers: New revenue procedure superseding Rev. Proc. 2018-32

related_question_answers.answer: Share independently verified public facts (re-fetched from IRS/OFAC sources) across sponsors; never share private evidence or approval decisions; known adverse public facts defeat Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance, so they should propagate.
Only after the platform independently re-verifies the fact from a primary source; the sponsor-originated correction is a lead, not evidence.
Propagate holds and verified public-source facts; never propagate sponsor-private investigation content (see RCD-029 dossier).

remaining_uncertainty: The 180-day interval is a business choice with no legal source; IRS could change publication cadence.
required_acceptance_criteria: Given the IRS posts a new monthly file, When a grant is released, Then the status check uses a snapshot built from that posting and records its posting date.
Given a charity appears on the Auto-Revocation List, Then pending releases to it are held for all sponsors.
Given a recipient is a group-exemption subordinate, Then the record is flagged 'reliance not available under Rev. Proc. 2018-32 §6.03'.
supporting_interpretation: Because IRS data change only about monthly, a check at approval and again at release against the latest published file suffices to obtain Rev. Proc. 2018-32 reliance; the 24-hour retrieval window ensures the newest monthly release is used. Reliance is per grant date, so a release-time check matters most.

alternative_design: Parameter-only design (no default dormancy disposition; every dormancy closure is a sponsor-approved task) - lowest exposure, higher sponsor workload (~1 manual review per dormant fund), no lost capability. Versus configurable default with A4 approval (recommended): low exposure, low friction.
applicability_to_unbound: Unbound must model per-person privilege state separately from fund state, carry per-sponsor configuration (nonresponse window, inactivity thresholds, default destination, successor generation caps, whether testamentary instructions are accepted), and never select a default destination itself.

authoritative_findings.claim: A DAF is owned and controlled by the sponsoring organization; advisory privileges are held by the donor or persons the donor appoints, so succession, dormancy and closure rules are matters of the sponsor's program terms, not of the donor's estate.

Fidelity: if no Successor named, balance goes to unrestricted funds on death of last Account Holder; a new Giving Account is created per Successor holding the allocated percentage; if no nominated Successor responds within 90 days the account terminates to unrestricted funds; no testamentary instructions accepted.

Vanguard Charitable: on death or incapacity of one advisor the remaining advisor retains privileges; succession is enacted only when the account is abandoned or on proof of the last advisor's death, incapacity or resignation.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Account structure p.3; Enacting a succession plan p.19

authoritative_findings.claim: DAFgiving360: succession activated only upon death or disqualification of all account holders; a new account per successor; executors/trustees cannot exercise privileges unless named successors.
NPT: Legacy Plan activates on written evidence of death of the last primary/joint advisor; six consecutive years without grant recommendations = abandoned, Legacy Plan applies.

Published inactivity triggers range from 2 years (Fidelity Trustee grants after two years without grants), 30 months (Vanguard, DAFgiving360 'inactive'), 30 months + 2 years (DAFgiving360 'dormant' then closure), 36 months (AEF review), 5 years (MS GIFT) to 6 years (NPT).
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Minimum grant requirements; EV-E-002 Minimum Account Activity; EV-E-003 inactivity; EV-E-004; EV-E-024/025 for AEF, MS GIFT

authoritative_findings.claim: Fidelity: grants to other DAF sponsors do not count as grant activity for its per-account minimum.
authoritative_findings.pinpoint: Minimum grant requirements - Each Giving Account

authoritative_findings.claim: No published sponsor text found addressing whether approved-but-unpaid grants proceed after the recommending advisor's death (OD-03); this remains a sponsor policy choice.

business_assumptions: Sponsors will configure their own thresholds; Unbound supplies defaults only.
Death verification uses documentary proof (death certificate) as sponsors require.
Escheat analysis (Q11) is limited to uncashed checks; fund balances are sponsor-owned and not unclaimed property of the donor (interpretation).
competing_interpretation: (1) Suspending the whole fund on the death of one joint advisor would contradict Vanguard and DAFgiving360 practice, where surviving advisors keep privileges; suspension should apply to the deceased person's privileges, and fund-level suspension only when the last advisor dies. (2) Some sponsors (Fidelity) act after two years of no grants, so a 48-month path may be looser than a sponsor's own aggregate-payout policy requires; the default must be overridable. (3) A charitable default 'per program terms' must not be the platform's choice: the sponsor's terms determine the destination (own pool, granting history, named charities).
consequences_if_wrong: Wrong fund-level suspension would freeze surviving joint advisors (customer harm, complaints); wrong default destination would breach sponsor terms and could misdirect charitable assets.
conservative_fallback: If sponsor has not configured a rule: suspend the deceased person's privileges, hold the fund's new grant intake pending sponsor review, and route any disposition to a sponsor approver (no automatic default).

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Suspend the deceased person's privileges; fund-level succession only when no living account holder remains.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Reads as fund-level suspension on any death; published sponsor practice (Vanguard, DAFgiving360, NPT) keeps surviving advisors' privileges and activates succession only when the last advisor dies or is disqualified.

corrections_to_prior_records.correction: Limit Q11 escheat validation to uncashed/voided checks; dormant balances follow sponsor program terms.
corrections_to_prior_records.issue: Fund balances are owned by the sponsor (§4966(d)(2)(A)(ii)); escheat analysis concerns uncashed grant checks, not dormant fund balances.
corrections_to_prior_records.record_or_artifact: RCD-022 validation_required ('counsel on escheat of balances (Q11)')

exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Donor death, succession, fractional allocations, dormancy, closure and outbound transfers.
external_authorization_required: Each sponsor's board- or management-approved program terms (succession, dormancy, default destination) loaded as configuration; no other external authorization identified.
jurisdiction: US federal (IRC §4966 ownership/control) plus sponsor program terms; state unclaimed-property law only for uncashed checks
landscape_update_candidates: Vanguard Charitable Jan 2026 policies: a durable POA is accepted as proof of incapacity to trigger succession (not as authority for the agent).
Vanguard Jan 2026: inactive after 30 months; minimum one $500 grant every three years.
original_provisional_answer: Adopt hold-on-notice, suspend-on-verified-death, then activate succession. OD-03: approved unpaid grants proceed unless sponsor policy says otherwise. Dormancy default: 36 months with no advisor activity, then 12 months of outreach on all verified channels and to successors, then a charitable default per the program terms (A4 approval). Closure and outbound transfer follow the state machines in UNB-RCN-ENT-005..007.
recommended_answer: Confirm with corrections: (a) Hold on credible notice applies to new advisor-initiated actions; on verified death suspend only the deceased person's privileges; the fund moves to succession only when no living account holder/advisor remains (or all are disqualified). (b) Successor allocations create one new fund per successor by percentage (rounding to the cent, remainder to the first-listed successor unless sponsor rule says otherwise) with a sponsor-configured successor-response window (default 90 days, the Fidelity published value; configurable up to 1 year per JCF); nonresponse routes to the sponsor's configured default. (c) OD-03: approved, unpaid grants proceed unless sponsor policy says otherwise (no published contrary rule found). (d) Dormancy default 36 months no advisor activity + 12 months outreach is acceptable as a configurable default within the 24-month-to-6-year market range; destination always comes from sponsor terms and requires the A4 approval. (e) Closure and outbound transfers per UNB-RCN-ENT-005..007; DAF-to-DAF grants do not count toward activity where the sponsor so specifies.
reconsideration_triggers: A sponsor publishes rules on approved grants after death
State legislation treating DAF advisory rights as estate property
Change in a sponsor's published inactivity thresholds
remaining_uncertainty: Individual sponsors' unpublished operating procedures; treatment of approved grants after death at sponsors that have not published a rule; state probate claims by estates (none found that override sponsor ownership).
required_acceptance_criteria: Given a fund with two advisors, When a verified death certificate for one is recorded, Then only that person's privileges are suspended and the surviving advisor can still recommend grants.

Given the last advisor's death is verified, When succession activates with successors at 50/30/20%, Then three new funds are created whose balances sum exactly to the source balance and the remainder cent rule is logged.
Given a named successor does not respond within the sponsor-configured window, Then the fund routes to the sponsor's configured default and requires sponsor approval before any distribution.
Given a grant was approved before death notice, When death is verified, Then the grant pays unless the sponsor policy flag 'cancel_approved_on_death' is true.

Given a fund has no advisor activity for the configured inactivity period, Then outreach starts on all verified channels and to successors, and no disposition occurs before the outreach period ends and an A4 approval is recorded.
Given a sponsor marks testamentary instructions as not accepted, When an executor submits a will-based instruction, Then the platform rejects it with a reason and records the document.
supporting_interpretation: The decided sequence (hold on credible notice, suspend on verified death, then activate succession) matches published practice in substance: every major sponsor activates succession only on proof (death certificate or written evidence) and only after the LAST advisor dies or is disqualified. Fractional successor allocations are standard (Fidelity, NPT, DAFgiving360 open one new account per successor). An approved grant is already the sponsor's decision, so letting it pay after the advisor's death is consistent with the sponsor's exclusive control (interpretation). The 36+12-month dormancy default falls within the published market range (24 months to 6 years).

alternative_design: Each sponsor sees only primary-source public data refreshed by the platform (no sponsor-originated signals): minimal legal exposure, loses early-warning value.
applicability_to_unbound: The platform is the conduit; it should propagate system holds tied to public facts and a neutral 'review requested' signal, never another tenant's private evidence.

authoritative_findings.claim: Grantors may not rely on IRS listings if they knew of, were aware of imminent, or were partly responsible for, a revocation; knowledge received from other sponsors could defeat reliance for the receiving sponsor.
Communications without malice to an interested person by one also interested are conditionally privileged (California).
Sponsors treat investigations of account holders as grounds to freeze accounts, showing investigation information is sponsor-held and sensitive.

Public facts are re-verified independently from the source before propagation (SPD-GRT-002).

Also, coordinated declines among sponsors could raise group-boycott (antitrust) questions (interpretation; not researched).
consequences_if_wrong: Propagating private allegations could bring defamation and confidentiality claims; failing to propagate public facts could lead to taxable distributions or grants to revoked charities.
conservative_fallback: Propagate only public-source facts; no inter-sponsor flags at all.
exact_question: Confirm provisional decision: Confidential sponsor investigations versus propagation of adverse charity findings.
